reference_use.conclusion: The pinned libraries supply the tools but none of the needed lemmas. SimonGMT has Simon's approximate tangent spaces with uniqueness and plane-support lemmas (Ch. 3), the injective weighted, Bochner and measure area formulas with Jacobian positivity, and a.e. uniqueness of within-derivatives (Ch. 2, AreaDomain). Mathlib has Rademacher, integration by parts for Lipschitz functions, L¹-density of C_c functions, smooth uniform approximation, Tannery's theorem, Lusin–Souslin and the μHE scaling and translation laws. No pinned or DAG declaration proves any of: uniqueness of approximate differentials along a set, weak-* convergence of gradients, the anti-Lipschitz bound for immersions, the chart pull-back, or the Leibniz rule with a Lipschitz multiplier. The dor_lmbsf_* analogues are decomposing and state different results. Hence there are nine new children, with the prefix dtc_bc_lc_sl_ll_ (absent from dag.json and git history), plus two accepted declarations reused with identical types: cmc_imRep_locality_restrict_sub (2af75d6) and cmcs_cd_defect_identity (e32f0ad). Four children need imports outside the base closure: ContinuousMapDense, SmoothApprox, Chapter02.WeightedArea/AreaCritical, Chapter02.AreaDomain and Tannery. Accepted candidates already add such imports. All 11 types elaborate in the contract-mode challenge header. Lean assemblies prove the parent type from weak_limit, smooth_leibniz, orient_interior, chart_pieces and lipschitz_smoothing, and prove weak_limit, piece_gradient, piece_weak_limit and smooth_leibniz from their declared dependencies, all with axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound only.

subproblem.title: Interior product of a unit simple (n+1)-vector with a 1-covector lies in its plane (supplied step 3)
subproblem.statement: Let P, n ∈ ℕ, ξ ∈ Λ_{n+1}(ℝ^P) (MultiVector P (n+1)) and α an n-covector on ℝ^P. For a 1-covector β put β∧α := alternatizeUncurryFin(β.smulRight α), i.e. (β∧α)(v₀,…,v_n) = Σ_i (−1)^i β(v_i) α(v₀,…,v̂_i,…,v_n). With e_i := EuclideanSpace.single i 1 and e_i♭ := innerSL ℝ e_i, put v := Σ_{i<P} ξ(e_i♭∧α)·e_i. Then (1) ξ(β∧α) = β(v) for every continuous linear β : ℝ^P → ℝ; and (2) if ξ is a unit orientation of a linear subspace Q (IsUnitOrientationOf ξ Q), then v ∈ Q.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P n : ℕ) (ξ : MultiVector P (n + 1)) (α : Covector (Euclid P) n), (∀ β : Euclid P →L[ℝ] ℝ, ξ (ContinuousAlternatingMap.alternatizeUncurryFin (β.smulRight α)) = β (∑ i : Fin P, ξ (ContinuousAlternatingMap.alternatizeUncurryFin ((innerSL ℝ (EuclideanSpace.single i (1 : ℝ) : Euclid P)).smulRight α)) • (EuclideanSpace.single i (1 : ℝ) : Euclid P))) ∧ ∀ Q : Submodule ℝ (Euclid P), IsUnitOrientationOf ξ Q → (∑ i : Fin P, ξ (ContinuousAlternatingMap.alternatizeUncurryFin ((innerSL ℝ (EuclideanSpace.single i (1 : ℝ) : Euclid P)).smulRight α)) • (EuclideanSpace.single i (1 : ℝ) : Euclid P)) ∈ Q
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source. Supplied proof of dtc_bc_lc_sl_lipschitz_leibniz, step 3, first and third bullets. This is Simon's computation in the proof of Ch. 6, Lemma 4.5(2) (chapter-06.txt lines 1281–1296, printed p. 156): "since ξ(x) orients T_xM, ⟨ξ, dh^{(σ)} ∧ ω⟩ = ⟨ξ⌞∇^M h^{(σ)}, ω⟩", stated pointwise. Here α plays the role of ω(x), and v is the vector of the interior product, so that ξ(β∧α) = β(v). The parent uses v(x) := θ(x)·v with α = ω(x), β = Dh_k(x) or β = H(x)♭.

Notation. β∧α := alternatizeUncurryFin(β.smulRight α), so (β∧α)(v₀, …, v_n) = Σ_{i=0}^{n} (−1)^i β(v_i) α(v₀, …, v̂_i, …, v_n) (ContinuousAlternatingMap.alternatizeUncurryFin_apply, with Fin.removeNth). e_i := EuclideanSpace.single i 1, e_i♭ := innerSL ℝ e_i = ⟨e_i, ·⟩, and v := Σ_i ξ(e_i♭∧α)e_i.

1. Linearity. β ↦ β.smulRight α is linear in β, and alternatizeUncurryFin is linear (alternatizeUncurryFin_add, alternatizeUncurryFin_smul, or the CLM alternatizeUncurryFinCLM). Composing with the linear map ξ, Λ(β) := ξ(β∧α) is a linear function of β.

2. Expansion of a 1-covector. For y ∈ ℝ^P, y = Σ_i ⟨e_i, y⟩e_i, since the e_i form an orthonormal basis of EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin P). Hence for every β ∈ (ℝ^P)*, β(y) = Σ_i β(e_i)⟨e_i, y⟩, i.e. β = Σ_i β(e_i)·e_i♭.

3. Proof of (1). By steps 1 and 2, and linearity of β:
 ξ(β∧α) = Λ(Σ_i β(e_i)e_i♭) = Σ_i β(e_i)ξ(e_i♭∧α) = β(Σ_i ξ(e_i♭∧α)e_i) = β(v).

4. Proof of (2), orthogonality. Suppose IsUnitOrientationOf ξ Q. Then there are an orthonormal family τ = (τ_0, …, τ_n) with span(range τ) = Q and a sign s ∈ {1, −1} with ξ(γ) = s·γ(τ) for every (n+1)-covector γ. Let b ∈ Q^⊥. By (1) with β := b♭ = innerSL ℝ b,
 ⟨b, v⟩ = b♭(v) = ξ(b♭∧α) = s·(b♭∧α)(τ) = s·Σ_{i=0}^{n} (−1)^i ⟨b, τ_i⟩ α(τ_0, …, τ̂_i, …, τ_n).
 Every τ_i lies in span(range τ) = Q and b ⊥ Q, so each ⟨b, τ_i⟩ = 0, and therefore ⟨b, v⟩ = 0.

5. Conclusion. By step 4, v ∈ (Q^⊥)^⊥ (Submodule.mem_orthogonal). Q is finite-dimensional, hence complete, so (Q^⊥)^⊥ = Q (Submodule.orthogonal_orthogonal) and v ∈ Q. ∎
proof_key_steps: β = Σ_i β(e_i)e_i♭ in the orthonormal basis; hence ξ(β∧α) = β(v).
For b ⊥ Q: ⟨b, v⟩ = ξ(b♭∧α) = ±(b♭∧α)(τ) = ±Σ_i (−1)^i⟨b, τ_i⟩α(τ without τ_i) = 0 (alternatizeUncurryFin_apply).
So v ∈ (Q^⊥)^⊥ = Q, since Q is finite-dimensional.

audit.reason: The basis expansion proves the pairing identity with the stated, unnormalized alternatizeUncurryFin convention. Evaluation on the orthonormal orientation annihilates every normal covector, yielding membership in Q by double orthogonal complementation.
